final_proof:
We use the following standard consequence of Ingham's theorem on gaps between consecutive primes.

**Prime-between-cubes lemma.** There is an integer \(M\) such that, for every integer \(m\ge M\), there is a prime \(q\) with
\[
m^3<q<(m+1)^3.
\]

Indeed, Ingham's prime-gap theorem states that there are constants \(C>0\), \(x_0>0\), and an exponent \(\theta<2/3\) (for example, any fixed \(\theta>5/8\) may be used) such that any consecutive sufficiently large primes \(p<p'\) satisfy \(p'-p\le C p^\theta\). Given a sufficiently large integer \(m\), let \(p<p'\) be consecutive primes with \(p\le m^3<p'\). Then
\[
p'-m^3\le p'-p\le C p^\theta\le C m^{3\theta}<3m^2+3m+1=(m+1)^3-m^3
\]
for all sufficiently large \(m\), since \(3\theta<2\). Thus \(m^3<p'<(m+1)^3\), proving the lemma.

Choose a prime integer \(a_1\ge M\), which is possible because there are arbitrarily large primes. Inductively, once the prime \(a_n\) has been chosen, apply the lemma to choose a prime \(a_{n+1}\) such that
\[
a_n^3<a_{n+1}<(a_n+1)^3. \tag{1}
\]
All the \(a_n\) are at least \(M\), so this recursion continues indefinitely. For every \(n\ge1\), define the closed real interval
\[
I_n=\left[a_n^{1/3^n},(a_n+1)^{1/3^n}\right].
\]
The left inequality in (1) gives
\[
a_n^{1/3^n}<a_{n+1}^{1/3^{n+1}}.
\]
Since the quantities in the right inequality of (1) are integers, it also gives \(a_{n+1}+1\le(a_n+1)^3\), and hence
\[
(a_{n+1}+1)^{1/3^{n+1}}\le(a_n+1)^{1/3^n}.
\]
Therefore \(I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n\). These are nonempty compact intervals in \(\mathbb R\), so completeness of \(\mathbb R\), in the form of the nested-interval theorem, shows that
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n\ne\varnothing.
\]
Choose \(A\) in this intersection.

It remains important to make the upper inequality strict. If \(a_{n+1}+1=(a_n+1)^3\), then
\[
a_{n+1}=(a_n+1)^3-1=a_n\bigl((a_n+1)^2+(a_n+1)+1\bigr),
\]
which is composite, contradicting the fact that \(a_{n+1}\) is prime. Thus
\[
(a_{n+1}+1)^{1/3^{n+1}}<(a_n+1)^{1/3^n}. \tag{2}
\]
For any fixed \(n\), membership of \(A\) in \(I_n\) gives \(a_n^{1/3^n}\le A\), while membership in \(I_{n+1}\), together with (2), gives \(A<(a_n+1)^{1/3^n}\). Hence
\[
a_n^{1/3^n}\le A<(a_n+1)^{1/3^n}.
\]
All quantities are positive, so raising to the power \(3^n\) yields
\[
a_n\le A^{3^n}<a_n+1.
\]
Consequently \(\lfloor A^{3^n}\rfloor=a_n\), which is prime, for every \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\). This proves the claim.
